title: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
description: Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health minist
body: Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.Footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.

schema.headline: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway

title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery
description: Image source, ReutersByNardine SaadBrad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vine
body: Image source, ReutersByNardine SaadBrad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce."We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.In the lawsuit, Pitt, 62, argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions."Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Jolie and Pitt wed at Château Miraval in 2014It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt's knowledge.Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip.Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged.Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being "too deferential" to their six children - aged eight to 15 at the time.Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle.It is understood that Pitt's litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Zahara Marley Jolie and Angelina Jolie at a film festival At the time of their 2014 marriage, Pitt and Jolie were among the most lucrative names in Hollywood.They met on the set of the 2005 film Mr and Mrs Smith and were soon dubbed Brangelina by the press.The marriage was Pitt's second after a relationship with Friends star Jennifer Aniston. It was Jolie's third, after actors Billy Bob Thornton and Jonny Lee Miller.Jolie adopted her first child, Maddox, from Cambodia in 2002 a few months after he was born. Pitt later adopted him after he and Jolie had begun their relationship.In 2005, the pair adopted daughter Zahara from Ethiopia when she was a few months old.The couple's first biological child, Shiloh, was born in Namibia in 2006.Their son Pax was adopted at the age of three from Vietnam in 2007, and twins Knox and Vivienne were born in 2008.Since the couple split, four of the six children have legally changed their last name to Jolie rather than Jolie-Pitt, according to court filings citied by Hollywood press.

schema.headline: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery

title: Trump’s accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
description: Image source, ReutersByThomas Copeland and Alison BenjaminBBC VerifyDonald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidi
body: Image source, ReutersByThomas Copeland and Alison BenjaminBBC VerifyDonald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.Image source, Getty ImagesNvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade.Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares.Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term.Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency."Additional reporting Becky Dale

schema.headline: Trump’s accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show

title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
description: Figure caption, Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin ReuterByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News InvestigationsA German
body: Figure caption, Watch: BBC confronts German boat dealer Marvin ReuterByJessica ParkerBerlin correspondent and Tom BealBBC News InvestigationsA German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police. Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A press photo from 2021 - migrants in a boat from Marvin Reuter's firm (logo circled) At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.Image caption, One night in May, French police stopped a car and seized boating equipment and fuel cansThe case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show."Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boatsBoth men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.Image caption, Part of the haul of dinghies and life jackets shown to us by German policeMeanwhile, further evidence has been gleaned from the bugging of a jail cell of a suspected gang chief, who is being held in pre-trial detention in France.Recordings captured the inmate talking about buying nautical equipment from a German firm run by a man with Reuter's first name: Marvin - according to files we have seen.The MaReBoote company address was also discovered on the alleged smuggler's phone, the case files say.Image caption, We confronted Martin Reuter at his company premises. We have blurred his face because of German privacy rulesWhen we confronted Reuter last month at his business in the town of Werne, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, he told us to leave and drove off.He then returned a short time later and said he was reporting us to the police. He did not answer our questions.We approached him in writing before and after this encounter including a detailed request for comment. In response to that request, he did not address the specific allegations but accused us of harassment.It is understood Reuter's lawyers have challenged his extradition, citing overcrowding in French prisons as one reason. Their client should face any allegations in Germany, they argue.Image caption, Reuter's firm is based in Werne, near DortmundIn Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

schema.headline: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds

title: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage
description: The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursd
body: The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings. The BBC said the partnership includes:A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecastsMet Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather appMore local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presentersMore "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climateThere will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".Separately, the BBC has dropped or shortened a number of national television and radio weather bulletins in recent weeks, as the corporation continues to work towards a £500m savings target.Some weekend and late-night forecasts have been dropped from the TV schedules, with regional presenters instead now delivering a UK-wide weather outlook during their presenting slots. Listeners have also complained about programmes such as Radio 4's PM no longer delivering a full weather bulletin, with presenter Evan Davis instead reading a short summary and directing listeners to the BBC website for a more detailed forecast. The BBC said it was changing its weather team to better serve digital platforms, in line with audience research and changing consumption habits. The corporation said more users are accessing weather information via the BBC's app, website and social platforms, as the number of people relying on broadcast bulletins declines.A spokesman for the corporation said: "The BBC is committed to providing a world-class public service for weather forecasting and information across our platforms."As we announced in July, we are making changes to the way we deliver weather information as more people are turning to mobile and the website for their weather forecasts. We also recognise that people want more local forecasts, along with the national picture, to help them plan their coming days more accurately."As such we are providing more digital and localised forecasts, as well as ensuring we still have appropriate national weather bulletins across the TV and radio."BBC Radio 4's Today programme, BBC Breakfast and the weekday editions of BBC One's News at Six will retain their usual national weather forecasts.

schema.headline: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage

title: The US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned
description: "Patriarchy is in accordance with the way God made the world." That is the view of Pastor Doug Wilson, a conservative minister who the US Secretary of
body: "Patriarchy is in accordance with the way God made the world." That is the view of Pastor Doug Wilson, a conservative minister who the US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth calls his mentor.Speaking to the BBC from his base in Moscow, Idaho, Wilson explained his view that a society led by men is "a very great blessing". It's a perspective Christians who disagree with him say is based on a fundamentalist understanding of the Bible, which promotes the subjugation of women.A self-described Christian nationalist, Wilson believes the US should be a theocracy, with gay sex criminalised, abortion outlawed, and people of other faiths unable to hold public office.In the past he has delivered a sermon on "The Lost Virtue of Sexism," arguing that the Bible says women should be excluded from leadership of the church, and certain roles in civic affairs. And as part of his views on the division between the sexes, he would like the 19th Amendment of the US constitution, which granted women the right to vote, to be repealed, something his detractors say is anti-democratic.The vast majority of Christians support women's right to vote, and dismiss his message as misogynistic and extreme.Rev. Canon Dana Colley Corsello, the vicar at the Washington National Cathedral, rejects Wilson's understanding of what the Bible says about women's roles."In my mind, there is no biblical precedent or standing for what [Wilson has] proposed," she told the BBC."I'm married, I have a husband, I have children. My husband and I are complete equals in everything we do."Have the American Pope and the American administration fallen out?Pete Hegseth brings combative style as face of Trump's war in IranBut while Wilson still represents a fringe perspective amongst Christians in the US, some of his views have been gaining support.The denomination he co-founded, the Communion of Reformed Evangelical Churches (CREC), has around 150 churches in the US. It's a drop in the ocean compared to the 350,000 or so other Christian congregations the US. But Wilson says membership continues to rise.His influence has grown in part because of his connection to Pete Hegseth. The Secretary of Defence is a "proud member" of a CREC affiliated church, a Pentagon spokesperson told the BBC, adding that the "secretary very much appreciates many of Mr. Wilson's writings and teachings".Wilson says the two have "a warm relationship", although he stresses it is "largely a pastoral one, not a political one". Wilson has led prayer services at the Pentagon, including one in mid-November.Joining Wilson on stage, Pete Hegseth said "thank you for your leadership, for your mentorship, for the things you've started, the truth you've told, your willingness to be bold."Hegseth worships at the Washington, DC branch of Wilson's network of churches. And there are other members of the current administration that worship there too, according to Wilson.Of all his views, it is his statements on women's suffrage that have garnered the most headlines.Wilson favours "household voting", where the head of the home – usually a man – votes on behalf of their family.  It's the system used for elections within his church, although the women in Wilson's family do vote in civic elections in order to counter votes of liberals, he says.He says only in "odd" circumstances,  such as divorce or bereavement or "where the husband was a quadriplegic," should women assume the role of head of household. Just 7% of votes in Wilson's church polity are cast by women.When challenged by the BBC, he admitted it was a system that gave men "outsized influence".Wilson says that repealing the 19th Amendment is "low" on the list of priorities for him and his congregation. But, he adds, "we do think it".Julie Ingersoll, a professor of religious studies at the University of North Florida, says Wilson's beliefs are misogynistic and extreme - part of a world view that says women should be in complete submission to men in every part of their lives.It is extremely unlikely that the 19th Amendment would be repealed - it would require either a proposal from two-thirds of the House and Senate or two-thirds of the state legislatures. Three quarters of states would then need to ratify it.Still, says Ingersoll, the threat to women's rights should be taken seriously."It's not unlike the battle that they waged against Roe versus Wade," she says, referencing the Supreme Court decision that granted women the right to an abortion. It was overturned in 2022, after years of legal battles that restricted women's access to abortion."Thirty years ago, people would have said, oh, they're not gonna undo abortion rights."But they chipped away and they kept chipping away until they were able to overturn it. And I see this as directly parallel."While Wilson says overturning the 19th Amendment could take a century or more, there are conservative Christians who are pushing for women to have their right to vote removed more immediately.Last February, pastor Dale Partridge posted on Instagram saying "We will repeal the 19th Amendment within ten years".Partridge, who has around 900k followers across social media, credits Wilson as being someone who "broke the ice" for "strong politics and theology".Partridge has said that "the majority of women are not capable of responsible voting" because too many of them are liberal.He also frequently collaborates on podcasts with another conservative pastor named Joel Webbon.Webbon, whose New Christian Right YouTube channel  has more than 190k subscribers, has said that women's "desires are wicked". The solution, he claims, is to "take away women's vote". He was once friendly with Wilson, although they have since fallen out."Those guys have overshot by a long way," says Wilson of the two younger pastors. "They are disruptors and basically rage baiting."So what might be driving those who support the effort?Kelly Marino, an associate professor at Sacred Heart University who studies women's suffrage, says that the last decade has seen big wins for the women's rights movement, and "liberal political ideology" in general.But, she argues, "any time where there was sort of this peak of feminism, there've been people who respond aggressively and try to push back".Added to that are the high levels of uncertainty and conflict that have characterised the post-Covid period."I think there's been this craving for tradition and things that felt safe," Marino says.That, she says, can be seen in the popularity of notions such as being a "tradwife" or "soft girl", who reject career goals in favour of traditionally female roles of wife and mother.Marino says that while she doesn't think the constitution could be changed in the immediate future, the conversation around repealing the 19th Amendment is shaping the way people think about women's roles in general.Canon Corsello, the Vicar at Washington Cathedral, sees the midterm election results as a repudiation of the push against women's rights."Cultural issues did not translate in this election", she says. "When people are preaching love, empathy, inclusion... that actually resonated with people".Wilson's views have, however, been gaining ground beyond the US. The CREC has more than 30 churches internationally, including in Poland, Japan and Brazil.The latter country has seen its own movement of right-wing influencers pressing for the removal of women's suffrage, with some leaning on religious language to make their point.Wilson wants to continue expanding his brand of Christianity around the world, and has recently accepted a church in England into his network.While CREC churches in each country have their own distinct characteristics, Wilson says their core beliefs are the same.When it comes to the US, he says his ideal scenario would be for his congregations to "to practice what we believe in the church and for outsiders to look at that and envy it and say, man, that seems like a good system".

schema.headline: The US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned

title: Newspaper headlines: 'Six-day streak "smashes" global temperature record' and 'Gord speed'
description: The Guardian says, external the world has, for the first time, experienced six consecutive days of average global temperatures 2C warmer than pre-indu
body: The Guardian says, external the world has, for the first time, experienced six consecutive days of average global temperatures 2C warmer than pre-industrial levels. The paper says the record hot streak started last week - and is continuing, which is likely to feed into growing concerns that global warming may be accelerating.The Daily Telegraph says, external the Ministry of Defence has written to about 100,000 military reservists asking them to update their contact details and provide information about their current jobs and skills. The paper says the move comes amid increasing threats from Russia. An Army source said there was no suggestion the reservists could be suddenly mobilised, and the aim was "to have a database and access" to them.The Times reports, external that the government's adviser on antisemitism, Lord Mann, is to investigate claims that the BBC is failing its Jewish staff. He says he has been told by whistleblowers about a "hostile work environment" in which they were pressed to show they were "a good Jew." The corporation says it has "introduced compulsory training on antisemitism" and actively encourages employees to report any incidences or concerns they have.US President Donald Trump's son in law, Jared Kushner, is quoted in the Telegraph, external as saying that Europe has yet to come up with a convincing plan to end the war in Ukraine. He said he had pushed Russian President Vladimir Putin "very hard" on the European position that there must be a ceasefire before any wider talks on European security, but the Russian leader "doesn't seem that interested."Andy Burnham is described in an editorial in the Sun, external as "our cringe-inducing Prime Minister," after an influencer posted what is described as a deeply offensive clip filmed just outside No 10. The paper says instead of looking cool, Burnham has trashed the dignity of his office and turned himself into a laughing stock. Downing Street has said the content was clearly not acceptable.The Daily Mail says, external people aged 70 and over will have to pass an eye test, every three years if they want to keep their driving licences. The paper says the change will be part of a major road safety shake-up.And the i Paper reports, external that the South Downs National Park is planning to create a new woodland the size of 800 football pitches, across Sussex and Hampshire. The paper says the project would have the carbon capture capability equivalent to the emissions of 54,000 petrol cars driven in England for a year.

schema.headline: Newspaper headlines: 'Six-day streak "smashes" global temperature record' and 'Gord speed'

title: Motorcycle catch: Man who caught a cricket ball on a moving vehicle found
description: "I told my friend riding the motorcycle to duck his head. I'm going to catch it."These are the words of Mehran Khan, who amazed sports fans around the
body: "I told my friend riding the motorcycle to duck his head. I'm going to catch it."These are the words of Mehran Khan, who amazed sports fans around the world when he caught a cricket ball while sitting on the back of a moving motorcycle.Mehran was passing a match in the Swat Premier League in Mingora when a ball sailed out of the ground towards him, with the passenger reaching out to catch it one-handed.Speaking to the BBC, he said of the grab, which has gone viral online: "I didn't think I would actually catch it." The employee of the Public Health Engineering Department was on his way home from work when he saw the ball being struck."I'm a cricket fan. I play cricket myself and I watch it too. I saw that Abrar Lala was at the crease and then he hit a six," he said."I told him [the friend who was driving] to duck his head. I'm going to catch it. Then I caught it."I made the effort, but I didn't expect to catch it. I thought it would fall somewhere nearby, but by the grace of God I managed to catch it."According to Mehran, immediately after the catch the Swat Premier League organisers announced a prize of 10,000 Pakistani rupees (about £27.60) for him, funded by the Pakistan Army.The Marghazar resident was caught by surprise when the recording of the catch spread so quickly online, saying: "The video went viral overnight. I didn't even know about it."He expressed his happiness at receiving the award, saying he was grateful to God, and added that he had returned the ball after taking the catch."People are saying I was taking the ball away with me, but that's not true. I returned it," he said.Swat Strikers won the match against GKR Dir by 34 runs, and Mehran urged the organisers to continue holding the tournament every year, describing it as an "excellent competition".

schema.headline: Motorcycle catch: Man who caught a cricket ball on a moving vehicle found

title: Stalking law simplified to become one offence
description: A new standalone offence of stalking is to be created in England and Wales after a review found the law regarding the crime was "cluttered and confuse
body: A new standalone offence of stalking is to be created in England and Wales after a review found the law regarding the crime was "cluttered and confused" - but the maximum sentence will not be increased.Specific stalking offences were introduced in 2012 but the underlying offence of harassment had to be established, and additional factors such as fear or distress proven, for it to be considered stalking.A review was ordered by the government last year, led by Richard Wright KC, who prosecuted the man who stalked and murdered Alice Ruggles in Gateshead in 2016.Victims of stalking have welcomed the change in law but said they were disappointed not all the recommendations have been adopted.Katherine, from Newcastle, whose former partner was arrested 28 times for stalking her, welcomed the government's decision to introduce one stalking offence instead of two. "I'm pleased about that one because my ex was charged with [the lesser offence] of stalking without fear to start with and I was terrified," she said."Anyone who's been stalked knows how terrifying it is, so that one [without fear] was just pointless."But her ex had resumed his behaviour after being sentenced to three years and four months in prison, and she criticised the length of jail terms given to stalkers, which she described as "an absolute joke and an insult to the victims".Ashley, from Washington, in Tyne and Wear, was also disappointed the maximum sentence would not be increased."Stalking can have a devastating and lifelong impact on victims and their families," she said."It affects your confidence, independence and ability to feel safe, even long after the relationship has ended and the perpetrator has been sentenced."Of the two current offences, only the more serious charge, which requires proof of fear of violence on at least two occasions, can be tried in the Crown Court, where the potential sentence is greater.The government has accepted the introduction of a single offence for stalking that can be tried in either Crown or magistrates' court and described it as the "biggest shake-up of stalking laws in more than a decade".But documents seen by the BBC show ministers rejected Wright's proposal to raise the maximum sentence from 10 to 14 years. Ministers said the average sentence for the more serious stalking offence in the year to March was 18.6 months, suggesting the existing maximum was not being fully used.Safeguarding minister Satvir Kaur said: "It's really important that victims know that we are holding perpetrators to account and feeling the full force of the law."The average sentences being given aren't good enough."She said judges were already able to jail stalkers for 10 years so it was better to work with them to make sure they used the powers available to them than "changing the goal posts" on the maximum sentence.The review was submitted to ministers earlier this year and last month Alice Ruggles's father, Clive Ruggles, said victims of stalking would be at greater risk of dying if the government failed to publish and act on the recommendations.Alice was killed in her Gateshead flat by her ex-boyfriend Trimaan Dhillon, who was found guilty of murdering the 24-year-old and jailed for 22 years.Her family has campaigned for better recognition of stalking and improvements in how it is tackled.Reacting to Thursday's announcement, Alice's parents said they "welcomed" the report and recommendations.They added they were "heartened" that the response "endorses the need for a single stalking offence that focuses on the perpetrator's behaviour and removes the onus on police and the CPS to prove the impact upon the victim".Wright's review concluded confusion between stalking and harassment laws could contribute to failures in identifying and prosecuting the crime.A previous investigation into police handling of stalking found three in every 20 stalking crimes examined had been incorrectly recorded as other offences, including harassment.The review also recommends removing the need for victims to demonstrate actual fear or serious disruption to their lives for a stalking offence to be established.Wright argues this would better protect victims who were unaware they are being secretly followed or monitored.The government said it would explore introducing such a test but had not yet committed to its inclusion in the new offence, although Kaur said she was "sick and tired of it being the onus on the victim".The review called for more consistent police investigations and greater use of specialist interventions to protect victims.It also raised concerns about stalkers using applications to change protective orders as a means of maintaining contact with, or control over, victims.Wright suggests additional safeguards, including requiring court permission before certain applications can proceed and ensuring victims can make representations.The government acknowledged the problem but said it needed to explore the suggestions further.Ashley, who was stalked by her former husband Jason Howe using an AirTag to track her movements, said she was "genuinely disappointed" by this response.Howe was jailed for three years and four months in March last year for stalking and controlling or coercive behaviour.But Ashley later discovered a restraining order designed to protect her had been amended, without her being consulted, allowing him to use a road through an exclusion zone near her home. "A restraining order is supposed to protect victims, not provide another opportunity for perpetrators to maintain control," she said.The government has decided not to adopt a recommendation that would allow previously convicted stalkers to face a new stalking prosecution after just one further incident involving the same victim.Instead, in previously announced legislation which comes into force on Thursday, courts will now be able to use stalking protection orders in cases of both conviction or acquittal."These orders can be in place for as long as is needed," Kaur said. The government said it would introduce the new legislation as soon as parliamentary time allowed, but had not set a date.Follow BBC North East on X, external, Facebook, external, Nextdoor and Instagram, external.

schema.headline: Stalking law simplified to become one offence

title: Aaron Rodgers: Pittsburgh Steelers release four-time MVP as starting quarterback
description: Veteran quarterback Aaron Rodgers may have played his last game in the NFL after being released by the Pittsburgh Steelers.In a brief statement publis
body: Veteran quarterback Aaron Rodgers may have played his last game in the NFL after being released by the Pittsburgh Steelers.In a brief statement published on Wednesday afternoon local time, the Steelers announced Rodgers, the NFL's four-time Most Valuable Player, was no longer with the franchise.That came hours after Rodgers appeared on US sports TV programme the Pat McAfee Show and confirmed his time with the Steelers was over."That ship has sailed," he said.Rodgers, who turns 43 next week, was also critical of Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy, including accusing him of snoring while he slept through team meetings.Shortly before the Steelers confirmed his release, McCarthy responded to that interview, telling reporters "there was an ultimatum made that was clearly outside his job description", adding it was his decision to let the player go.All this came after the Steelers had said on Tuesday that Mason Rudolph will be their starting quarterback for Friday's home game against the Denver Broncos.The Steelers added that Rodgers would be inactive for the game, so would not serve as back-up to 31-year-old Rudolph.McCarthy was in charge of the Green Bay Packers for most of Rodgers' 18-year spell in Wisconsin, including their Super Bowl win in 2011.Rodgers, who joined Pittsburgh in 2025 after two years with the New York Jets, was "99% sure" he was going to retire after leading the Steelers to last season's play-offs.However, McCarthy's appointment by Pittsburgh persuaded him to play one more year.But Rodgers told the talk show on Wednesday the season had not been "what I signed up for".Although the Steelers have a 6-4 record, they have suffered two straight defeats after losing 19-16 at the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday.When asked about a potential change on Monday, McCarthy said "Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback".But a day later the Steelers announced that is no longer the case - and now they have gone a step further.Pittsburgh's brief statement confirming Rodgers' release, external is likely the unceremonious end to an illustrious career.While Rodgers was unable to claim a second Super Bowl win, he was named the season MVP in 2011, 2014, 2020 and 2021. Only Peyton Manning (five) has won the award more times.Rodgers insisted his 22nd year in the NFL would be his last, and he has been let go at a crucial stage in the season.The Cincinnati Bengals (7-3) lead the AFC North division, with Pittsburgh third, but with seven games left the Steelers occupy the final play-off spot for the AFC Conference.Although Pittsburgh are 6-4, they have had to grind out some of those wins as they have struggled offensively. They rank 22nd for both points and passing yards per game.Rodgers is undoubtedly past his best, but his form has only dropped slightly from last season and the team's struggles are by no means entirely down to him.The Steelers' depth among their wide receivers is thin. Michael Pittman is out injured and DK Metcalf has not delivered the production expected when he was brought in with Rodgers before the 2025 season.Metcalf, 28, was even ejected during Sunday's loss at Philadelphia, meaning Rodgers had to lean on debutant Max Hurleman with the game on the line.And it is not as if Pittsburgh had a hot-shot rookie quarterback pushing for an opportunity to impress.Rudolph is in his ninth season and has started each as a back-up. After being drafted by the Steelers in 2018, he joined Tennessee for the 2024 season then returned to Pittsburgh, starting 19 of his 38 career games.McCarthy is hoping Rudolph can spark his offence, but if he doesn't, would they revert to the two young quarterbacks on their roster?Teams seldom make such a sudden change at this stage in the season, especially those with a winning record and a quarterback of Rodgers' stature.Rodgers has clashed with team management, team-mates and coaches throughout his career - including McCarthy - but the latest of those fallings out is certainly not the farewell one of the greatest quarterbacks of all time was hoping for.

schema.headline: Aaron Rodgers: Pittsburgh Steelers release four-time MVP as starting quarterback

title: 'All coming together' - Isak repaying Liverpool faith
description: When Isak scored his opener against Club Brugge, it marked a sixth consecutive away game in which he has struck.That meant he joined an exclusive club
body: When Isak scored his opener against Club Brugge, it marked a sixth consecutive away game in which he has struck.That meant he joined an exclusive club of just eight players to have achieved that feat, following in the footsteps of Dick Forshaw, Sam English, Gordon Hodgson, John Evans, John Aldridge, John Barnes and Mohamed Salah.Isak has now scored the joint-most away goals across all competitions this season (eight – level with Erling Haaland). His total is also already more than any Liverpool player managed away from home in the 2025-26 campaign (six by Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Virgil van Dijk) and it is only November.Isak looks to be brimming with confidence, exemplified by his second goal as he latched on to a pass from Alisson to go through one-on-one and then chipped a confident finish past the goalkeeper. But for Andoni Iraola, Isak's performance offered much more than goals, the Liverpool manager also praising the striker's overall contribution."He is in a great moment right now," he said."In the first half especially he helped us with the link up. In the second half it was more about defending a little lower."It is not just Isak who is looking the part in the Liverpool attack.Florian Wirtz continued his impressive run of form with a goal that means he now has eight goal contributions in his last five games for Liverpool and Germany."Both are now in a good place," Iraola said of Wirtz and Isak."When the team overall is playing well and we are getting good results everything looks a little better."The important part if they help the team to play well and get results. Alex and Florian right now are in a good moment."But the Liverpool attack as a whole is looking dangerous, regardless of who plays along with Isak and Wirtz. In Wednesday's 3-0 win, it was Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola who completed the front four, while in Sunday's 4-0 defeat of Manchester United it was Rio Ngumoha who played in Munoz's position."We have so many good players in our team," Wirtz told TNT Sports. "Even when we can substitute some wingers, midfielders or strikers in the 60th minute or later it gives us a lot."It shows how good our team is and it is important for a top team to have a strong bench."Liverpool's win against Club Brugge was their seventh from their last 10 games across all competitions."I spoke to Wirtz at the weekend, after the [Manchester] United game, and we were talking about his form - and he said 'well it helps that the team are playing well'," Warnock added."It's true because if you try to influence a bad team or a team that's not playing well, then it is much harder."With a fitter Isak, Wirtz looks a better player because now he is playing balls in behind that Isak is getting to, and getting in on goal on the back of."It has a knock-on effect, which is obviously like Wirtz said, he is playing in a team which is better equipped to suit him."

schema.headline: 'All coming together' - Isak repaying Liverpool faith

title: Wang Fuk Court: A renovation was meant to improve these Hong Kong homes - it ended in a blaze that killed 168
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The fire was one of Hong Kong's deadliest in decades ByGrace TsoiBBC World ServicePhoebe KongBBC Chinese Repo
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The fire was one of Hong Kong's deadliest in decades ByGrace TsoiBBC World ServicePhoebe KongBBC Chinese Reporting fromHong Kong and Yvette TanIt was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user -  was trapped inside their home."I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said. Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second -  an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Lau Man Kwong took care of his grandson before his death (blurred at source)"It was ferocious… I saw the fire jump [from one building to another] - then a huge fireball burst. It was truly hell on Earth. How could anyone possibly escape?" said Mrs Lau.She tried calling her husband again. This time, there was no answer.The body of Lau Man Kwong was eventually found by rescuers - he had locked himself inside the toilet."He was wearing his slippers, sitting on the toilet and clutching his identity card," said his wife, who added that she escaped death "by the narrowest margin"."I would have held onto my husband and died with him."He was such a good person. I just don't understand why he had to die in such a terrible way."Mr Lau and his wife moved into Wang Fuk Court in 1983 - the year the building was completed.She recalls an idyllic life - a family with three children who were able to grow up close to the sea and spend weekends playing at a nearby park."All three of my children adored my husband… He could be very stern, and I was the only woman who could make him laugh."No way out In 2024, mandated renovations began in Wang Fuk Court.In Hong Kong, all buildings over 30 years old have to undergo an inspection - and any necessary renovations as a result.Like many building complexes in Hong Kong, Wang Fuk Court had a management committee that oversaw things like building repairs. As many as 57 construction companies submitted bids. But the company that won, Prestige Construction and Engineering (PC&E), submitted the most expensive bid at HK$336m ($42.8m; £32.4m).Residents, many of whom were over 65, had to bear the cost. The hefty bills triggered protests but eventually, the contract was signed. But once the renovations began in July 2024, residents were unhappy.Among the complaints was that workers constantly smoked on site, dropping cigarette butts everywhere.The 1,154 page report suggested the fire was caused by a lit cigarette.Figure caption, Watch: Christy says she still sends WhatsApp messages to her husband who died in the blazeThere were also complaints about most of Wang Fuk Court's eight buildings having their windows taped over with foam boards to stop debris falling in - blocking daylight or any sort of view at all, for months.All eight buildings were also covered in a protective mesh netting and bamboo scaffolding.The report also found that after typhoons damaged the original scaffolding nets in 2025, cheaper non-fire-retardant replacements were chosen - something that was done as a "cost-saving measure at the expense of the safety of the residents".Residents had filed nearly 140 complaints to six government departments, including the fire services and the buildings departments, in and after 2024, but these were largely ignored, the report went on to say.It also revealed that a staff member of the estate's property manager, ISS, had turned off the power supply to the fire alarms in all eight buildings - which is why no alarms rang on the day itself.ISS later told the BBC it had "reviewed and reinforced its procedures [and] staff training" in Hong Kong, adding that it takes the findings of the report "very seriously".But for those who did manage to flee their homes - the emergency staircase turned out to be another death trap. Windows were removed from some fire escape stairwells to create temporary openings for workers - letting in smoke and cutting off vital escape routes.Dozens, including Christy's husband, died in such stairwells. Image source, Lam Yik / BBC ChineseImage caption, Christy's daughter celebrated her ninth birthday the day before the fireChristy, who wanted to be identified only by her first name, says her husband was at home alone when the fire broke out. She only found out about it when her friends sent her messages about it. By the time she made it to the apartment complex, it was already cordoned off.She found out later that he had died of smoke inhalation in the stairwell, something she says that is at least of some consolation to her."My husband's body would have been burnt and he would have been in more pain if he was at home. At the very least… his suffering was minimal."Christy says her family had just celebrated their eldest child's ninth birthday the day before - they had saved some leftover cake in the fridge to eat the next day. Their father never got to eat it. Both children have been deeply affected by the loss of their father. Her youngest child, a seven-year-old boy, had "covered his ears and yelled" when he was first told what had happened to his father.He now often comforts his mother, saying he will take care of her as he is the only man in the family."He hides his emotions. A seven-year-old child should not behave this way, and I feel heartbroken," says Christy, who has herself been diagnosed with PTSD and depression.Her daughter has "extreme thoughts" she says, and channels her emotions through art. She turned 10 on Wednesday, but this year, there was no birthday celebration in sight. Her birthday, she says, will now instead be a day to commemorate her father.Bid-rigging and rubber stampsWang Fuk Court's problems date back to before the renovations began.The management company hired to oversee and supervise the project, Will Power, conspired with PC&E to defraud residents in Wang Fuk Court, according to the city's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).Although PC&E was found to have breached safety requirements and violated building department rules for multiple previous projects, homeowners at Wang Fuk Court were told that they had a clean record.The ICAC alleges that this was part of a lucrative scheme, with Will Power's director Wong Hap-yin, along with other individuals, laundering over $5m in suspected proceeds from the tendering process from Wang Fuk Court, among other housing projects.Once PC&E cinched the contract, Will Power's registered inspector - an individual meant to oversee the renovations - merely rubber-stamped the documents, without having actually conducted any inspections personally, the report added.Will Power has been since liquidated and PC&E could not be reached for a response.Both companies - Will Power and PC&E - and seven individuals have been charged with 25 counts of offences including including manslaughter, conspiracy to defraud, attempting to pervert the course of public justice and tax evasion.Four of them are still in custody but none of the cases have gone to trial yet.The report said both companies involved were the "main culprits responsible".But it also directed heavy criticism at authorities, saying that "no government department took effective ownership of various fire safety issues and complaints about fire hazards fell into a vacuum".One expert, Prof John Burns of Hong Kong University, had called the event the "largest governance crisis" that authorities have faced since 2020 - a reference to the controversial National Security Law that was passed in that year.On the day the report was released, almost one year after the fire, Hong Kong's housing chief Winnie Ho resigned and the city's top leader John Lee apologised for the first time, promising that a "large number" of reforms would be rolled out.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Homeowners at Wang Fuk Court (pictured) were told their construction company had a clean recordA shell of a homeFive months after the fire, Mrs Lau was allowed into her flat for the first time to collect any personal belongings that might have remained.In her first visit, she was given just three hours to retrieve 40 years' worth of belongings.Pictures taken from the visit show a home that has been utterly burned out - with every surface blackened and soot covering the floor."I almost fainted when I saw what had become of my home. I don't understand how the home I had built, such a warm and beautiful home, could end up like this," said Mrs Lau.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, The frame of Mr Lau's wheelchair was one of the few things left in their burnt homeHer children, who came with her, described the house as a "war zone". Among the rubble, they found broken pieces of a piggy bank that Mr Lau had dutifully filled with coins every day for the past 20 years."Everyone in our family knew it was his favourite possession. The piggy bank died with him," said Mrs Lau.Mrs Lau and her daughter have since rented a place nearby to live - and she is worried about how she is going to afford a new house. The government has said it will spend $867m (£663m) to acquire affected flats - but Mrs Lau says it is not nearly enough to buy a similarly sized flat in the area.Still, her family was in a better position than many others, she said."Should I say that we are fortunate?"I lost my husband but many families lost multiple family members... Babies less than a year old died. "Stories have emerged of some of the other victims - a six-month-old who died alongside her 68-year-old grandmother when the fire broke out. The bodies of an Indonesian domestic helper and the elderly person she worked for were found huddled together.Image source, BBC Chinese / Phoebe KongImage caption, Mrs Lau's son has since bought new piggy banks in memory of his fatherAs for Christy, she says she is planning to file a lawsuit against those responsible for the fire - but acknowledges that even if she wins, she "can't [get] my husband's life back"."I share things that happen in our daily life, as if he still existed," she says. "I often write to him, 'I miss you so much. Are you doing well on the other side?'"It's a similar story for Mrs Lau, who says she can't go anywhere without seeing her husband."Every day, something reminds me of him," she said."I still find it very hard to accept that my husband is gone, my home is gone, and so many of my neighbours are gone…. This place was my roots. I never imagined it would also mark an ending for me."

title: Andy Taylor obituary: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off
description: In 2022, it was announced that he had advanced prostate cancer, the same disease that had killed his father. Le Bon spoke for the remaining members of
body: In 2022, it was announced that he had advanced prostate cancer, the same disease that had killed his father. Le Bon spoke for the remaining members of the group. "It's absolutely devastating," he said.Taylor avoided chemotherapy, believing it would affect his guitar playing by weakening his fingers. Instead, he embarked on an experimental "nuclear therapy", which he hoped would give him five more years of life.Initially, at least, it seemed successful but, a year later, Le Bon said his former bandmate's disease was a  "very late, fourth-stage metastasised cancer".In 2025, Taylor managed to release a third solo album, Man's a Wolf to A Man. Urged by Tracey to express himself for a final time, he even provided the vocals.For Andy Taylor, that first train ride down to Birmingham had been like entering Narnia in the Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe.Overnight, he had gone from serenading strippers in northern clubs to a rock-star lifestyle with the world's most popular band.So, was the rollercoaster ride worth it? Taylor answered his own question in his autobiography, published in 2008."Maybe if there'd been fewer lows there wouldn't have been so many highs," he wrote. "If I had to do it all over again, I don't think I would have changed a thing."Though next time I'll give a miss to swallowing all that elephant's piss," he added.
